replying_to: Replying to Prompt-Based Metric Learning for Few-Shot NER
display_title: Official Review of Paper4356 by Reviewer G4fG

content.confidence: 4: You are confident in your assessment, but not absolutely certain. It is unlikely, but not impossible, that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work.
content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper presents a new framework for few-shot named entity recognition. The framework is based on metric learning, with token-level similarity scores calculated for each query token and all those in a support set. The token representation is produced by weighted-averaging the tokens from multiple mask-reducible instances (i.e., the instances augmented with prompts such that the original input sentence could be recovered via appropriate masking) induced from different prompting schemes. With a solution built on previous work (CONTaiNER; Das et al., 2022), experiments on different few-shot NER settings have shown some promising results with metrics surpassing the state-of-the-art numbers by a non-trivial margin.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
- There seems to be some novelty in the proposed scheme to leverage multiple prompted input with the property of being "mask-reducible"
- Empirical superiority against previous methods on various evaluation protocols

Weaknesses:
- The strength of ensembling multiple prompts has not been explored to a reasonable depth since: (1) there are only two types of prompts studied in this work, and (2) weighting is controlled by $k-1$ tunable hyperparameters for combining $k$ prompts which does not seem to be flexible.
- It seems difficult to interpret what makes the proposed framework working much better than previous work.
- (Actually a common weakness from relevant literature on few-shot NER) The few-shot settings in the currently experimented benchmarks are all simulated instead of naturally occurred real scenarios.
- The task setting is over-specific to the main stream of ICLR, henceforth more suitable to be submitted to an NLP venue.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Personally I like the experimental settings and the evaluation protocols (episode-based evaluation alone is too far from low-resource scenarios in practice), and actually would like to see this paper appearing at an NLP conference for more in-depth discussion in that community after non-trivial revision.

To clarify for the second weaknesses above more specifically:

The qualitative analysis does not seem to be sufficient since it does not cover multiple evaluation settings or provide non-trivial insight on why ProML behaves differently from other systems in comparison.

Additionally, currently there are only two types of prompts being used, and one of which (prompt A) actually only helps label space reduction while losing too much useful information in mention boundaries. However, in the ablation results it seems that keeping prompt A only outperforms keeping prompt B only. This seems counterintuitive.

Moreover, from the current study, readers may find it difficult to get which part of the experiments could support the claim that "ProML is a general framework consistent with any token-level metric learning method and can be easily plugged into previous methods" as stated in the conclusion section.

Minor: In the beginning of Sec 3.1 the NER task has been stated as a sequence labeling task. This statement is incorrect since there have been many different formulations such as span prediction or even question answering.
content.summary_of_the_review: This submission has a certain level of technical novelty in solution design and has reported empirically superior performance against previous work, but currently fails to clearly convey the most important messages on why the framework should work better. The studied task (few-shot NER in English) is also rather specific even for an NLP conference.
content.correctness: 2: Several of the paper’s claims are incorrect or not well-supported.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.

display_title: Official Review of Paper4356 by Reviewer 8BLw

content.confidence: 4: You are confident in your assessment, but not absolutely certain. It is unlikely, but not impossible, that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work.
content.summary_of_the_paper:
This work addresses the problem of leveraging label semantics in few shot NER. One line of previous work on few-shot NER is based on the idea of computing token-level similarities between query and support sets in an embedding space. However, such works don't explicitly incorporate label semantics in the learning of the embedding space. The current work argues that label semantics can potentially help few-shot NER if it is incorporated in the learning of the embedding space. It proposes to leverage label semantics by using multiple prompts as input to the transformer-based architecture for learning the embedding space. Specifically, it proposes two types of prompts - option prefix and label-aware). Each of these prompts are constructed from the input token sequence by inserting either label options (option-prefix prompt) or ground truth labels (label-aware prompt) to the original input sequence. Insertion is done in a deterministic manner in each case with the help of a predetermined mask. The prompts are  mask-reducible in the sense that the positions of the tokens in the prompt can be determined from the mask. In the learning phase, both prompts are used as input to the transformer-based learning architecture. Learning comprises of feeding each prompt to a length-preserving transformer (with shared parameters), taking the average of the masked output of the last four hidden layers as the intermediate representation of the corresponding prompt, computing a weighted average, and projecting the token representations to obtain Gaussian embedding. Similar to Das et al. (2022), a contrastive loss function is used. In the query phase, only option-prefix mask is used and the resulting prompt is fed into the corresponding transformer. Labels are assigned to the query sequence by finding the nearest neighbour of each of the query token among all support tokens in the embedding space. 

The work presents experimental results for two formulations of few-shot NER: tag-set extension and domain transfer. It uses OntoNotes 5.0 dataset (three splits) and FewNERD dataset in the evaluation of tag-set extension formulation. It uses OntoNotes 5.0 dataset as the source domain, CoNLL’03, WNUT’17, I2B2’14, and GUM as target domains in the evaluation of domain transfer formulation. It compares the results of the proposed approach with multiple baselines including Das et al. (2022) whose extension this work is. The improvement in F1-score across all the different experiments is very encouraging.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
The idea of forming prompts by inserting labels into the input sequence is interesting.
The two prompt schemas employed in the work are simple to implement and use. 
Experimental evaluation is systematic and empirical improvement over multiple baselines on several datasets is very encouraging.

Several questions regarding the methodology and evaluation are left unanswered. They should be addressed by the authors to make the paper more readable, complete, and solid.

	1. How are label options determined for a given input sequence? At the time of learning, all entity types in the ground truth label sequence could be possibly used as label options. However, at query time, ground truth sequence is not available. 
	2. Is it assumed that entity labels are always single token (e.g. person, city, age, etc.)? How do you handle multi-token entity types? (e.g. religious leader, terrorist organization, government agency, political party, etc.)
	3. Why are separators like ',', '[', ']', '|' used in the prompts? (see Figure 1) What happens if they are removed?
	4. In the option-prefix prompt function does the order in which the label options are concatenated make a difference to the learning of the embedding and to the results?
	5. In Table 3, isn't "plain" the same as CONTaiNER? Or are there significant differences? 
	6. In Table 3, plain + B does significantly better than plain, A and B. Can you explain why as this is counter-intuitive: B has all the information that plain has and more. 
	7. In Table 3, there are no results reported for plain + A. Why?
	8. In Appendix A.1, what are the two axes representing? There are no labels in the graph.
	9. In Section 5.2 it is stated, on the basis of Figure 3, that the proposed approach suffers less from overfitting than the baseline (CONTaiNER). However, it is not clear why this is so and no explanation is provided. 
	10. From Figure 3, it seems that both the proposed approach and the baseline  (CONTaiNER) are overfitting for FewNERD-INTRA than FewNERD-INTER. Why?
	11. In Figure 2, is the colour-coding of entity types consistent?
	12. Both in Table 3 and Table 5, A (option-prefix prompt) performs better than B (label-aware prompt). This means that augmenting the input sequence with label options (global) is better than augmenting the tokens in the input sequence with entity  types (local). Can you explain why?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
It is not motivated in Introduction either through actual examples or by reasoning why label semantics can be useful for few-shot NER. More specifically, some discussion is needed on what is the additional information that labels contain which can be useful for few-shot NER.

Title is somewhat misleading as the main contribution is the design and use of prompts in few-shot NER. There is no new contribution to metric learning aspect of few-shot NER relative to Das et al. (2022).

There is not much novelty in the methodological aspects of the proposed work. 

Experimental is systematic and the improvements are very encouraging. 

As the proposed approach is both simple and easy to implement, it should be easy to reproduce the results.
content.summary_of_the_review: The submitted work proposes to leverage label semantics in few-shot NER through prompts. It gives two simple schemas for prompts and shows through extensive experimental study that incorporating label semantics in the learning stage can lead to very encouraging improvements in the results. There are some questions/concerns that are not addressed by the work, the proposed method is very simple and should be of interest to both researchers and practitioners.
content.correctness: 3: Some of the paper’s claims have minor issues. A few statements are not well-supported, or require small changes to be made correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.

content.confidence: 4: You are confident in your assessment, but not absolutely certain. It is unlikely, but not impossible, that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work.
content.summary_of_the_paper: The authors propose ProML as a metric learning method to solve few-shot named entity recognition. This paper largely follows previous ACL2022 paper "CONTaiNER: Few-Shot Named Entity Recognition via Contrastive Learning". In the original CONTaiNER paper, a contrastive loss is optimized to reduce the distance between Gaussian embeddings of tokens from the same NER class, and increase the distance otherwise. This submission attempts to further inject label semantics into the Gaussian embeddings. To achieve that, the authors apply two types of modifications onto the original sentence, which are (1) listing all entity class names ahead of the input sentence, and (2) inserting entity class names right after each entity token. A token's representation is then the weighted sum of representations from the two modified sentences. Similar to CONTaiNER, given a query token at inference time, the proposed method finds its nearest neighbour in the support set, and uses the NER label of the support token as the prediction of the query token.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
1. Overall, the paper is well-written and well-organized. The authors provide thorough background and explanation of terms.
2. The proposed method shows promising improvement over the chosen baselines, provided that the results are reproducible when the code is released.
3. There is detailed ablation on the option prefix prompt and label-aware prompt, as well as the choice of weight coefficient to balance them.

Weaknesses:
1. It is unclear how option prefix prompts help to generate better representations. The authors explained they "inform the main model of which labels to predict", but how does listing all the entity class names help to pull same-class entities together and push different-class entities apart?
2. When label-aware prompts are applied, a positive pair of tokens have the same inserted label name in their vicinities. Thus, the model is likely to yield representations that emphasize the label names, but neglect the important semantics of the entity token itself. As a result, the model would fail to generate good representations of query tokens, which do not have label names inserted.
3. Following Weakness #2, there is a discrepancy between representations of support tokens and query tokens, as query tokens do not use label-aware prompts. During training, token representations use both option prefix prompt and label-aware prompt, and the distance between such representation of tokens is optimized. Therefore, it does not make sense to find the nearest neighbouring support token of a query token.
4. NER is extremely class-unbalanced, with the majority of tokens being non-entity ("O"). Therefore, the distribution of "O" is widespread and might mess up the nearest neighbour search. Thus, it is important to show the distribution of "O" in Figure 2 visualization, which the author intentionally excluded for unknown reasons.
5. It should be noted that OntoNotes contains news domain data, which coincides with datasets such as CoNLL. Therefore, using them as a domain transfer pair might not be suitable.
6. From Table 3, label-aware prompts present reduced performance compared to the plain baseline. The authors explained that OntoNotes has many numerical types that label-aware prompts might not generalize well too. However, this issue is also present for option prefix prompts, and cannot explain why label-aware prompts are not working.
7. On OntoNotes datasets, option prefix prompt (A) and label-aware prompt (B) alone lead to reduced performance or only marginal improvement compared to the plain baseline. However, how does the weighted sum of A and B suddenly demonstrates substantial improvement? Besides, a "plain + A" configuration should also be explored.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: Overall, novelty of this paper needs to be improved. The proposed method follows previous CONTaiNER (ACL2022) and only attempts to inject label semantics by inserting label names into the input sentence. However, the two types of insertion used (option prefix prompt & label-aware prompt) are not well-motivated, and it is not well-explained why they help to improve upon the original contrastive learning method of CONTaiNER, as mentioned in Weakness #1 & #2.
content.summary_of_the_review: This submission improves upon ACL2022 paper "CONTaiNER: Few-Shot Named Entity Recognition via Contrastive Learning", by injecting label semantics via option prefix prompt and label-aware prompt. However, design of the two prompts are not well-motivated and justified. Furthermore, the discrepancy between support and query tokens causes problems for nearest neighbour search at inference. Overall, the novelty of this paper needs to be improved.
content.correctness: 2: Several of the paper’s claims are incorrect or not well-supported.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.

content.confidence: 4: You are confident in your assessment, but not absolutely certain. It is unlikely, but not impossible, that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work.
content.summary_of_the_paper: In this study the authors investigate metric learning for few shot learning (FSL) for named entity recognition (NER). In metric learning for FSL NER the support set is compared token-by-token with  the tokens of the test cases. The tuple of (support token, test token) with the largest inner product (or some other similarity function) is used to determine the labels for the tokens of the test cases. To enhance the performance of this approach the authors propose the simple idea to add the label information as a text, e.g. adding the text "organization" next to the tokens that are labelled as ORGANIZATION (i.e. mask reducible prompt based metric learning). They can show that their approach is quite effective, i.e. they improve by a large margin over other meta-learning approaches for FSL NER.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
S1. The approach is simple.

S2. According to their experiments their proposed approach is very effective. 

W1. The paper is written in an overcomplicated way to convey a fairly simple idea. 

W2. They claim that label semantics is what helps in their approach (i.e. the meaning of the words in the label). This could have been investigated by replacing the label names with meaningless sequences of characters or by using a randomly sampled word. This could have shown to what extend the label's words did help in their approach.

W3.  The split of Ontonotes were unclear (what classes were left out?) It is really difficult with such a small amount of classes to construct meaningfully varied episodes.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The authors provide details about the training, but some details about the dataset splits for Ontonotes are unclear. The biggest problem is the structure of the paper: it is difficult to read, some notations are not explained and crucial concepts the paper uses in the introduction are only explained later in Section 4. Using the name "prompt" in the approach is highly misleading, and mainly alludes to the fact that the authors believe their approach to be working because it could exploit the information in the label names, how it was observed in prompt-baed learning.
content.summary_of_the_review: In its current state the quality of the paper in terms of writing and experiments is not sufficient to be published at ICLR.
